opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, because it really is hard and expensive. But for us, the answer comes down to what we're actually trying to build. Our goal isn't a slightly better autocomplete or a nice wrapper around someone else's model. We want an AI that can do the work of a software engineer, and eventually help us do AI research itself. If that's the goal, you can't treat the model as a black box you rent from someone else.

The things we think matter most aren't really available off the shelf. Long context is a good example. We care a lot about a model being able to hold your entire codebase, your documentation, your history, everything, in its head at inference time, rather than relying on retrieval hacks or fine-tuning for every customer. Getting that to work well isn't a prompting problem. It touches the architecture, the training data, the infrastructure, how you serve it efficiently. You have to control the whole stack to push on it properly.

There's also the question of where the leverage is. If you only build the product layer, you're betting that whatever the frontier labs ship happens to suit what you need, and that you can differentiate on UX. Maybe that works for some companies. But if you believe, like we do, that the model itself is where most of the value and most of the progress comes from, then not training your own means you've outsourced the most important part of your company.

And yes, it's risky. It costs a lot of money, you need a lot of compute, you need a team that can do pre-training at scale, which very few people in the world have done. But the way I see it, the bigger risk is building on a foundation you don't control and finding out in two years that the thing you actually needed was never on anyone else's roadmap. If we're right about where this is going, the payoff is enormous. If we're wrong, at least we were wrong trying to do the thing that matters. I'd much rather take that bet.

r001.rationale: The response says that relying on frontier labs would leave Magic betting on their models and differentiating only on UX, while outsourcing the model itself—the part it sees as most valuable. This conveys the lack of a distinct contribution if the provider solves the core problems.

r002.rationale: It says training costs a lot and is risky, but does not say that the investment cannot be recovered if training fails.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss personal enjoyment of training as a reason to spend investors’ money.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is probably the question I get asked most often, and I think the honest answer is that it's not a choice we made because we wanted to, it's a choice we made because the mission requires it.

Magic's goal is to build something that behaves like a colleague, not an autocomplete. If you want a system that can actually work inside a codebase the way an engineer does, it needs to see the whole thing. Not a retrieved snippet, not a summary, but the actual repository, the documentation, the history of the conversation, all of it at once. That pushes you toward context windows that are orders of magnitude beyond what the frontier labs were designing for. And when you need an architectural property that nobody else is optimizing for, you can't get it by fine-tuning on top of someone else's API. The attention mechanism itself has to be different. The way you handle memory has to be different. Those are decisions that get made at pretraining time, and if you don't control pretraining, you don't get to make them.

The second reason is more strategic. If you build on top of another lab's model, your ceiling is their roadmap. They decide what gets prioritized, they decide the pricing, they decide what the model is good at. We'd be a thin layer whose entire differentiation could disappear with a single release from someone else. I don't think you can build a durable company, let alone something that meaningfully changes how software gets made, in that position.

And then there's the research argument. Some of the things we care about, like whether a model can actually reason over a very long horizon and stay coherent, are open scientific questions. You can't answer them from the outside. You have to be able to run the experiments, change the training mix, change the objective, and see what happens.

Now, is it hard? Absolutely. Is it financially frightening? Yes. Training runs are expensive, the engineering is brutal, and if you get it wrong you've burned a lot of capital. But I'd rather take a risk on the thing that could actually work than take a safer path that structurally caps what we can become. The way I think about it, the downside of training your own models is that you might fail. The downside of not training them is that you can't succeed at the thing you set out to do. Given that, the decision was less agonizing than people assume.

r001.rationale: The response says dependence on another lab’s API would make Magic a thin layer whose differentiation could disappear with one release from that provider.

r002.rationale: It says failed training runs are expensive and would mean burning a lot of capital, communicating that the training spend cannot be recovered.

r003.rationale: The response says training is required by the mission, but does not address personal enjoyment as a reason or whether that would justify risking investors’ money.

astra-6.text:
For us, training models is a means to an end. The goal is to build an AI that can do substantial software engineering work, and that requires more than generating a good snippet of code. It needs to understand a large codebase, work through a problem over many steps, and check whether what it did actually works.

If we build entirely on someone else’s model, we can improve the surrounding product, but we’re dependent on their decisions about what the model learns and which capabilities they prioritize. Training our own gives us the ability to work on those capabilities directly and develop the model and the product together.

That’s a difficult and expensive bet. But the question is whether taking that risk is necessary to reach the goal. Our view is that it is. We’re not trying to train models just to say we have our own models; we’re doing it because we think the core intelligence still needs to improve for the product we want to build.

r001.rationale: The response says relying on another model would make Magic dependent on the provider’s choices, but does not say Magic would lack a distinct contribution if that provider solved the fundamental problems.

r002.rationale: It calls training a difficult, expensive bet, but does not say the spending cannot be recovered if training fails.

r003.rationale: It says Magic is not training models merely to have its own, but does not address personal enjoyment as a reason or risking investors’ money.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, it starts with what we’re trying to build: an AI that can work with you on an entire software project. That requires more than generating a good answer to a prompt. It needs to understand a large codebase, keep track of what it’s doing, and work through problems over long periods of time.

If we rely entirely on someone else’s models, we’re depending on their research priorities lining up with those requirements. We can build a lot around a model, but there are limits to what you can fix at the application layer. We want to be able to change the training itself when that’s what the problem calls for.

Obviously, that’s a difficult and expensive path. But the question is whether the easier path can actually get us to the product we want to build. Our view is that owning the model research gives us the ability to pursue the capabilities that matter for that mission.

r001.rationale: The response says external models may not align with Magic’s needs, but does not say Magic would lack a distinct contribution if a provider solved the fundamental problems.

r002.rationale: It calls model training difficult and expensive, but does not say that spending would be unrecoverable if training failed.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss personal enjoyment or whether that would justify risking investors’ money.
